title: Self Assessment deadline 31 January 2027: what to do now
description: File your 2025/26 return and pay by 31 January 2027. Payments on account, penalties, what directors need and a dated checklist.
author: Barry Adams
why: People search for the Self Assessment deadline from December until 31 January every year. This gives the site its own timely guide for clients and prospects instead of relying on the syndicated news feed.

html:
Your 2025/26 Self Assessment tax return must be filed online by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027, and any tax you owe must be paid by the same time. For most freelancers, sole traders and company directors, that payment is the balance of your 2025/26 bill plus the first payment on account towards 2026/27. Start now and you'll avoid the January rush, the £100 late-filing penalty and a nasty surprise on the bill.

This guide walks you through who needs to file, how payments on account work, what to gather, and a dated checklist from now to the deadline.

Who needs to file a 2025/26 tax return?

The 2025/26 tax year ran from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026. According to HMRC's guidance, you must send a return if, in that year:

  • you were self-employed as a sole trader and earned more than £1,000 (before expenses)
  • you were a partner in a business partnership
  • you had Capital Gains Tax to pay
  • you had to pay the High Income Child Benefit Charge (income over £60,000) and don't pay it through PAYE

You may also need one if you had untaxed income, such as rent, savings interest, foreign income or dividends. That last one catches most limited company directors, which we cover below.

If HMRC has written asking you for a return, you must file one, even if you think you owe nothing. If you've stopped trading or no longer need to file, tell HMRC rather than ignoring the letter.

Your 2025/26 return matters for another reason too. HMRC uses it to decide who joins Making Tax Digital for Income Tax. If your combined self-employment and property income was over £30,000 in 2025/26, you'll need to use MTD from 6 April 2027. Our Making Tax Digital guide explains what that means.

What's due on 31 January 2027

Two things share the same deadline:

  1. Your online return for 2025/26. The paper deadline was 31 October 2026, so if you haven't filed yet, it has to be online.
  2. Your payment. This is usually your balancing payment for 2025/26 plus your first payment on account for 2026/27.

31 January 2027 is a Sunday. HMRC says payments need to reach it by the last working day before the deadline, unless you pay by Faster Payments or by debit or credit card. If you pay by Bacs (three working days), plan for it to land by Friday 29 January. You can check all the options on GOV.UK's pay your bill page.

Payments on account, explained simply

Payments on account are advance payments towards next year's bill. Each one is half of the previous year's Self Assessment bill (including Class 4 National Insurance if you're self-employed). They're due on 31 January and 31 July.

You don't have to make them if your last bill was under £1,000, or if more than 80% of your tax was already collected another way, for example through your tax code.

A simple worked example

Say your bill for 2024/25 was £4,000, so you paid two payments on account of £2,000 towards 2025/26 (in January and July 2026). Your actual 2025/26 bill comes out at £6,000.

Due dateWhat it's forAmount
31 January 2027Balancing payment for 2025/26 (£6,000 minus the £4,000 already paid)£2,000
31 January 2027First payment on account for 2026/27 (half of £6,000)£3,000
31 January 2027Total to pay£5,000
31 July 2027Second payment on account for 2026/27£3,000

This is why your first year of self-employment can feel brutal. If you had no payments on account the year before, you pay the whole bill plus half of it again in the same January.

If your income has dropped in 2026/27, you can ask HMRC to reduce your payments on account, online or with form SA303. Be careful, though. If you reduce them too far, HMRC charges interest on the shortfall.

Penalties for filing or paying late

HMRC's late penalties build up quickly.

Late filingPenalty
1 day late£100
3 months late£10 a day, up to £900
6 months late5% of the tax due or £300, whichever is higher
12 months lateAnother 5% or £300, whichever is higher

Paying late costs extra too: 5% of the unpaid tax at 30 days, another 5% at 6 months and another 5% at 12 months. On top of that, HMRC charges interest on anything unpaid, currently set at the Bank of England base rate plus 4%.

So file on time even if you can't pay in full. If you owe up to £30,000 [CONFIRM: current online payment plan limit] and have filed, you may be able to set up a payment plan online. Interest still applies, but you avoid the filing penalties.

What records to gather

Everything you need relates to 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026. Start pulling together:

  • your business income: invoices, sales and any platform payouts
  • your business expenses: receipts, bills, mileage logs, home-working costs
  • your P60 or P45 if you were also employed, and any P11D for benefits
  • dividend vouchers from your own company or any shares you hold
  • savings interest and rental income
  • pension contributions you made personally, and Gift Aid donations
  • Child Benefit details if your income was over £60,000
  • details of anything you sold that might create a capital gain

Keep your records for at least five years after the 31 January deadline. For your 2025/26 return, that's until at least January 2032.

If you're a limited company director

Being a director doesn't automatically mean you need a return. What matters is your income. If you pay yourself a small salary through payroll and the rest as dividends, your dividends usually push you into Self Assessment, because the tax on them isn't collected through PAYE.

For 2025/26, the rules were:

  • a £500 dividend allowance
  • dividends taxed at 8.75% in the basic rate band, 33.75% in the higher rate band and 39.35% in the additional rate band
  • dividends inside your unused personal allowance (£12,570) taxed at nothing

From 6 April 2026, the basic and higher dividend rates rose by two points to 10.75% and 35.75%. Your 2025/26 return uses the old rates, but your payments on account for 2026/27 are based on your 2025/26 bill. If you take similar dividends this year, those payments may fall short, and you'll have a bigger balancing payment in January 2028. It's worth putting a little extra aside now.

Common mistakes we see every January

  • Leaving your HMRC sign-in to the last minute. If you've forgotten your Government Gateway details, getting back in can take time.
  • Thinking the bill is just last year's tax. The first payment on account often makes January's payment far bigger than people expect.
  • Forgetting smaller income. Savings interest, a bit of rent or dividends from shares all need to go on the return if they're taxable.
  • Missing allowable expenses. Mileage, phone, software and professional fees all reduce your profit.
  • Forgetting the High Income Child Benefit Charge if either partner's income went over £60,000.
  • Falling for scam emails and texts. They peak around the deadline. Our guide on how to spot HMRC scams shows what to look out for.

If you spot a mistake after you've filed, you can correct your 2025/26 return within 12 months of the deadline, so until 31 January 2028.

Your checklist from now to 31 January

ByWhat to do
End of November 2026Check you can sign in to your HMRC online account and find your UTR. Start gathering the records listed above. Get your 2025/26 bookkeeping finished. If we do your return, send us your information as early as you can.
Mid December 2026           Check the figures. Decide whether to reduce your payments on account if your income has fallen. Submit your tax return with time to prepare for paying your bill.
Friday 29 January 2027Last working day before the deadline. Make sure Bacs payments have reached HMRC.
Sunday 31 January 2027Online return and payment deadline, 11:59pm.
31 July 2027 Deadline for you Second payment on account for 2026/27.

Questions people ask

What is the Self Assessment deadline for 2025/26?

31 January 2027 for online returns and for paying what you owe. The paper return deadline was 31 October 2026.

What happens if I miss the deadline by a day?

You'll get a £100 late-filing penalty. If it's still not filed after three months, daily penalties of £10 start, up to £900, and further penalties follow at six and twelve months. Late payment adds 5% penalties and interest.

Do I have to make payments on account?

Only if your last Self Assessment bill was £1,000 or more and less than 80% of your tax was collected at source. If both apply, you pay half of last year's bill on 31 January and half on 31 July.

Do company directors need to file a tax return?

Not automatically. You'll usually need one if you take dividends above your allowances, or have other untaxed income. If your only income is a salary taxed through payroll, you may not.

I'm a sole trader. Does Making Tax Digital change this deadline?

Not for 2025/26. You still file your return by 31 January 2027. But if your 2025/26 self-employment and property income was over £30,000, you'll join MTD from 6 April 2027 and send quarterly updates too. See our sole trader accountants page for how we help.
